candidate_originals.stem:
A Massachusetts pharmacist reviews outpatient labels and proposed substitutions. Assume the prescriber’s intended ingredient, strength, dosage form, and route are known. Each option describes a separate work-queue record. Assume all other prerequisites are satisfied; judge the action and facts actually stated, not an unstated exception.

Which proposed actions are supported by the applicable requirements? Select ALL that apply.

choices.text: A pharmacist applies a shorter product-specific in-use period when it is more limiting than the general label-date ceiling.
A pharmacist preserves the actual prescribing practitioner in internal verification records while using an eligible protected-care practice name on the patient label.
A pharmacy treats the statutory ten-characters-per-inch wording as an automatic requirement for ten-point type.
A pharmacist treats a private note to the inventory department as the required patient notification after biological substitution.
A pharmacist recognizes that a required federal patient-to-patient transfer warning does not prohibit a lawful pharmacy-to-pharmacy prescription-information transfer.

candidate_originals.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist receives a prescription for a brand-name biological product. The prescriber has not prohibited substitution. The pharmacy has a less expensive FDA-licensed biosimilar, but FDA has not determined that product to be interchangeable with the prescribed biologic. May the pharmacist substitute that biosimilar under Massachusetts' statutory biologic-substitution authority without obtaining new prescriber authorization?

choices.text: Yes, because every FDA-licensed biosimilar is automatically interchangeable for pharmacy substitution.
Yes, because the absence of a prescriber prohibition is the only condition Massachusetts imposes.
No. The statutory substitution pathway requires an FDA determination that the substitute is interchangeable with the prescribed biological product.
No, because Massachusetts prohibits pharmacist substitution of any biological product.
Yes, but only if the patient waives notification to the prescriber.
